lesson.title: The Body's Own Painkillers: Endorphins and Natural Analgesia
lesson.summary: Endorphins are the brain's own opioid like chemicals, neuropeptides that bind the same receptors as morphine and heroin to reduce pain and produce feelings of relief or pleasure. They explain why intense stress or exertion can blunt pain in the moment, and why opioid drugs are able to hijack a system the body already has.
lesson.body:
The name endorphin is short for endogenous morphine, and it describes exactly what these chemicals do: they are neuropeptides, a class of larger neurotransmitter molecules made and released by neurons, that act on the same receptor systems targeted by opioid drugs like morphine. Unlike small, fast acting neurotransmitters, neuropeptides such as endorphins are typically released in a more modulatory role, shaping how strongly other signals come through rather than firing off single quick messages of their own.

Endorphins act primarily by binding opioid receptors, most notably a subtype called the mu opioid receptor, found throughout the brain and spinal cord. When endorphins occupy these receptors, they generally reduce the activity of the neuron they are acting on. One especially important target of this effect is the release of substance P, a neuropeptide that carries pain signals into the spinal cord. By binding opioid receptors on the terminals of pain sensing neurons and reducing how much substance P those neurons release, endorphins dial down the intensity of the pain signal at its very first relay point in the central nervous system, before it can even travel further toward conscious awareness.

This system makes sense from a survival standpoint. Pain is adaptive most of the time, since it demands attention and withdrawal from whatever is causing tissue damage. But in a genuine emergency, being overwhelmed by pain could be fatal: an animal fleeing a predator while injured needs to keep moving despite the damage. A surge of endorphin release during intense stress or exertion allows pain to be temporarily muted so the body can keep functioning until the immediate threat has passed. The same release is also associated with mild feelings of pleasure or relief, which is part of why endorphins get folded into popular explanations of the so called runner's high after sustained vigorous exercise, though researchers note that other systems, including the body's endocannabinoids, likely contribute to that experience as well, so it is probably not endorphins acting alone.

Opioid drugs work precisely because they mimic what endorphins already do. Morphine, heroin, and oxycodone all bind the same opioid receptors that endorphins naturally activate, but often more strongly and for a longer duration, producing more intense and more sustained pain relief and euphoria than the body's own system typically generates. Because the body regulates its natural endorphin production and receptor sensitivity based on ongoing signaling, repeated exposure to these external opioids can cause the natural system to scale back, contributing to tolerance, in which larger doses are needed to achieve the same effect, and to withdrawal, in which pain sensitivity and discomfort spike once the drug is removed and the body's own system has not yet recovered.

One more distinction is worth noting alongside the reuptake mechanism covered earlier. Because endorphins are peptides rather than small molecule transmitters like serotonin or dopamine, they are not typically cleared from the synapse by dedicated reuptake transporters pumping the intact molecule back into the presynaptic neuron. Instead they are broken down by peptidase enzymes within the synaptic space, a clearance strategy closer to how acetylcholine is degraded than to how classic reuptake works.
